overview: Imagine paddling toward Tenochtitlan in 1495. Canoes crowd canals beside white-plastered houses; traders unload maize, cacao, cotton cloth, feathers and obsidian; two aqueducts bring spring water toward a city built in a lake. At the center, bright temples rise above markets, schools, workshops and neighborhoods. This power was not one simple “Aztec nation.” Tenochtitlan’s Mexica rulers worked with Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance, while hundreds of altepetl, local city-states, kept their own leaders, rivalries and traditions. Armies and tribute tied the patchwork empire together, often harshly, but unconquered Tlaxcala and the Purépecha state resisted it. The atlas shows only 1492 to 1500 and calls the feature “Mexihcah.” Historically, the alliance began around 1428, continued past 1500 under the separate atlas id aztec-empire, and was broken in 1521 by a huge Indigenous-Spanish coalition, siege, hunger and epidemic disease. Colonial manuscripts preserve Nahuatl voices, pictures and memories, but they were made after invasion and must be read beside archaeology. Mexica imperial rule ended; Nahua peoples, languages, arts and communities did not.

periods.title: Three lake powers defeat Azcapotzalco
periods.summary: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan formed an alliance during war against the Tepanec center Azcapotzalco. Sources vary between 1427 and 1433 for formal arrangements, so 1428 is a useful convention rather than a signed modern constitution date.

periods.title: Tribute networks expand before the map slice
periods.summary: Successive rulers expanded military and tributary power while many conquered altepetl retained local rulers. Tenochtitlan became the strongest partner, yet autonomous rivals, resistant frontiers and patchy corridors kept the empire from becoming one solid territorial block.

periods.title: Ahuítzotl begins an expansionist reign
periods.summary: Ahuítzotl ruled Tenochtitlan from 1486 to 1502. He enlarged sacred and hydraulic works and launched campaigns before the atlas feature begins, placing the 1492 start inside a continuing reign rather than at a foundation event.

periods.title: The exact atlas window
periods.summary: The indexed mexihcah-triple-alliance polygon exists only for 1492 to 1500. Campaigns toward Oaxaca and Tehuantepec and tribute from distant places occurred in this window, but the feature also encloses unconquered Tlaxcala and other autonomous communities.

periods.title: The same polity receives a different atlas id
periods.summary: At the 1500 seam the target vanishes and aztec-empire appears with a different polygon. Historically the Triple Alliance continued, Ahuítzotl ruled until 1502, and Motecuhzoma Xocoyotzin then governed Tenochtitlan; no empire was refounded in 1500.

periods.title: Coalition, epidemic and siege break imperial rule
periods.summary: Spanish forces entered a landscape of rival Indigenous states in 1519. Tlaxcalan, Texcocan, Huexotzincan and other armies became essential to the coalition; smallpox, defections, blockade, lake warfare and siege preceded Tenochtitlan’s capture in August 1521.

sections.title: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly

items.text: The exact indexed id is mexihcah-triple-alliance, displayed “Mexihcah (Triple Alliance),” circa 1492 to 1500. The coverage ledger classifies it as a state with one border file, one observed interval, no researched card, no review, and no override. This packet fills that exact missing record.

A separate indexed id, aztec-empire, already claims the historical Triple Alliance from 1428 to 1521 and has a short researched card. The two ids are not successive countries: they are overlapping database identities for the same imperial system. “Mexihcah” most directly names the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, not every allied or tributary people.

At 1492 the target is one Polygon with one part, one ring and 109 coordinate positions. Its bounds are [-101.94761947619476,16.34168785177978,-94.8159481594816,21.885411342450965]. The raw-coordinate SHA-256 is dbc0cc19bd3c57b16d53c1deead14005d9cba135a368feb9f7390789ff3f517d; its rotation-and-direction-independent canonical hash is c6dcd8c3548ba39e982307c627ff0292c909544c7a6ea83ac913f7b9ec83c392. Those decimals measure encoding, not political certainty.

Point tests put Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan, Cempoala, Oaxaca, and wrongly unconquered Tlaxcala, inside the ring. It excludes the Purépecha capital Tzintzuntzan, Tehuantepec, Tapachula and independent Tututepec. It also overlaps Nahua, Cholulteca, Otomí, Totonac and Binnizá display polygons. That is imported map layering, not proof those peoples became Mexica.

Neither alliance id appears at 1400. At 1500, mexihcah-triple-alliance disappears and aztec-empire appears as a 49-position polygon with bounds [-105.5080550805508,16.172741995985177,-93.74313743137431,22.895904517527384], raw hash 116fcd553f02270465c02f0690d8dec426c2fe9da9c88dc9129d2bfca1a1a8d8 and canonical hash e5678e9b2d0575027ac720f102b6761881aee6b2e82cd112d3b3f1d389259d2f. By 1530 every tested point is mapped as New Spain.

The alliance emerged from a war that overthrew Azcapotzalco around 1428. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan brought different dynasties, armies and claims into the partnership. Later sources disagree about the exact moment and original bargain, so historians reconstruct formation from traditions rather than reading a surviving treaty signed by all three rulers.

The core partners were not one ethnic unit: Mexica ruled Tenochtitlan, Acolhua ruled Texcoco, and Tepaneca ruled Tlacopan. Each capital had its own tlatoani, or speaker-ruler. A royal serpent labret from the wider region connects powerful speech, mouth ornaments and office, but one elite jewel cannot describe ordinary government.

Tenochtitlan became the dominant partner, yet “emperor” can hide negotiated rule. Many subjected altepetl kept local dynasties and laws if they delivered tribute and military help. Garrisons or governors appeared in some strategic places, while other districts were linked through clients, roads or fear. The empire was powerful because it was flexible, and vulnerable for the same reason.

An altepetl was a local political community tied to land, water, patron deities and a ruling house. The Triple Alliance usually ruled through these communities rather than replacing every council. Tribute collectors, judges and local nobles stood between households and distant capitals, so a farmer in Oaxaca did not receive daily orders straight from Tenochtitlan.

Colonial tribute manuscripts picture cotton cloth, warrior suits, feathers, cacao, rubber, gold and other deliveries from named provinces. They are invaluable, but the Codex Mendoza was commissioned around 1541 to 1542 under Spanish government. It recalls an earlier system through Indigenous painting and colonial annotations; it is not an untouched 1495 treasury spreadsheet.

sections.title: The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade

items.text: The entire atlas window lies inside Ahuítzotl’s reign, 1486 to 1502. Archaeology assigns Templo Mayor phase VI, the House of the Eagles and flood-repair floors to this era. The king enlarged institutions already built by predecessors; 1492 did not start his government, the alliance, Tenochtitlan or Mexica history.

Ahuítzotl’s forces campaigned against Huaxyacac in 1494 and toward Tehuantepec in 1497, while long-distance merchants and frontier politics reached Soconusco. Control remained thin and contested in the far south. A tribute list or garrison can show pressure without proving continuous occupation of every mile between the capital and coast.

Tlaxcala resisted conquest and endured a long Mexica economic blockade. Its city falls inside the atlas polygon anyway, making the ring historically wrong at a crucial point. Tlaxcalan leaders later chose alliance with Cortés for their own political reasons; calling them merely Spanish helpers erases an independent state and its strategic choices.

The Purépecha or Tarascan state defeated a major Mexica invasion and defended a fortified western frontier. Tzintzuntzan correctly falls outside the target point test, but a smooth polygon still cannot show contested marches, empty buffer zones, raids or shifting client towns. Imperial strength had a hard western limit.

Pochteca merchants organized long journeys from central Mexican cities and moved feathers, stones, cloth and other costly goods through linked markets. Their routes also created diplomatic knowledge and danger, but not every merchant was a state spy. The Florentine account is a later Nahua history of merchant institutions, not a trip diary from 1495.

sections.title: A lake city was an engineering project

items.text: Tenochtitlan grew on islands and reclaimed shallows. Straight causeways joined it to shore, canals carried canoes through the city, and neighborhood streets connected houses, workshops and shrines. This was not a city that merely “floated”: builders drove stakes, moved fill, laid stone, repaired embankments and continually negotiated soft lake mud.

Chapultepec springs fed connected cisterns and channels, then aqueducts carried fresh water toward the capital. Sacred meanings and practical engineering met in the same system. Archaeological and historical work also shows unequal delivery: elite districts and palaces had better conduits, while many commoner households depended on water carriers.

Waterworks could fail spectacularly. Sources blame Ahuítzotl’s Acuecuexco project for a devastating flood, and excavated temple precinct floors show repeated raising against subsidence and inundation. Engineers managed risk; they did not conquer it. The lake gave transport, food and fertile mud while constantly threatening foundations and drinking supplies.

At the Templo Mayor, paired stairways led to shrines of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, connecting war, rain, food and Mexica state ceremony. Rulers repeatedly enclosed earlier stages inside larger ones. Modern excavation therefore reads a layered building, not one frozen pyramid; many colonial structures now sit above the buried precinct.

Stoneworkers quarried, hauled, pecked, ground and polished volcanic and other stones using stone or hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand. Sculpture could be brightly painted, so today’s gray museum surfaces are incomplete. Monumental carving demonstrates skilled teams and supply chains, not metal saws, secret lasers or effortless royal magic.

sections.title: Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands

items.text: Chinampas were long constructed plots raised from shallow lake beds with mud, vegetation and retaining edges; calling them “floating gardens” is catchy but physically misleading. Canals gave access and moisture. Archaeologists have uncovered a canal-and-field complex under modern Mexico City, while Xochimilco preserves a living descendant landscape.

Xochimilco became a major tributary and food supplier after conquest by Tenochtitlan. Its farmers and boat crews retained local identities and interests; in 1521 some lake towns changed sides under pressure. A cabbage-shaped green patch on a map cannot show who owned a plot, rowed a canoe or decided which army to feed.

Tlatelolco’s market served the paired island cities and offered regional food, cloth and luxury goods. Specialized sellers and officials organized exchange, while smaller towns held their own markets. Tribute entered storehouses through political obligation; market trade involved negotiated exchange. Mixing them together makes every cacao bean look confiscated, which the evidence does not support.

Palace stores held dried maize, beans, chia, amaranth, salt, chile and squash seeds, supervised by stewards and tribute gatherers. These records reveal institutional reserves, not the exact pantry of every family. Common meals centered on maize foods with beans, squash, chiles and local greens; access to cacao, meat and luxury foods varied sharply.

Long-distance goods could move by human carriers and canoes because Mesoamerica had no draft animals or wheeled freight system. That limitation encouraged dense route knowledge, relay labor and valuable lightweight cargo. Obsidian blades, salt, pottery and food moved alongside feathers, gold and greenstone; ordinary necessities mattered even when museums display jewels.

sections.title: Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood

items.text: Nahua society distinguished nobles, commoners, merchants, priests, warriors, dependent laborers and enslaved people, but these were not modern race boxes. Rank affected land, clothing, schooling, courts and tribute. Military achievement could bring status to some men, while debt or punishment could create dependency; local practice differed across the empire.

A calli meant both a house and a household world; relatives, spouses, children and dependents shared work and ritual. Neighborhood communities often organized land and service. Colonial household records are richer after 1521 than before it, so historians should not turn one ideal family picture into a universal rule for residence or marriage.

Women ground nixtamal, cooked, spun and wove; many also traded in markets, served temples, managed property or worked in specialist households. Men dominated high imperial offices and warfare. These were strong gender expectations, not proof every woman or man did identical work, and colonial writers often squeezed complex lives into moral examples.

Codex Mendoza scenes show boys carrying loads or fishing and girls grinding maize or weaving, with dots marking ages. The pictures make household teaching vivid, but Indigenous artists made the manuscript around 1541 to 1542 for a colonial patron. They describe remembered norms and stages, not surveillance footage of every child before 1500.

Young people learned first through household work and oral instruction. Later accounts describe telpochcalli linked to commoner neighborhoods, calmecac for elite and priestly learning, and institutions for girls. Curricula joined discipline, song, ritual, rhetoric, calendrics, public labor and warfare. Attendance, ages and access varied; “universal school” is too confident.

sections.title: Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power

items.text: The Templo Mayor joined Huitzilopochtli, Mexica patron of war and solar power, with Tlaloc, an older rain and fertility deity worshiped across Mesoamerica. That pairing linked conquest to agriculture. Subject communities kept many local gods and rites, so “Aztec religion” should not flatten hundreds of altepetl into one identical belief system.

Mexica specialists coordinated a 260-day ritual count with a 365-day seasonal count; their combinations repeated over a 52-year cycle. The festival year included eighteen twenty-day periods plus additional days. Colonial correlations to European dates remain debated, and a calendar organized farming and ritual without functioning like a modern weather app.

Human sacrifice was real, public and politically meaningful. Excavation of the Huei Tzompantli found postholes and a circular skull-built element, with studied remains including men, women and children from phases 1486 to 1521. Archaeology confirms killing and display; it does not automatically confirm every huge total reported by later writers.

Authentic colonial Nahuatl sample from the 1577 Florentine Codex, Book 9: diplomatic transcription “Izcatqui in iuh tlamanca in ie uecauh.” Normalized spelling: “Izcatqui in iuh tlamanca in ye huecauh.” Translation: “Here follows the way in which things were long ago.” It introduces a Nahua account of merchant history.

The sample is alphabetic Nahuatl written after invasion by Indigenous collaborators in a Franciscan project; it is not a preconquest codex line. “Normalized” means modern editors regularized colonial spelling, not that the sound is certain. Preconquest tlacuiloque also used pictorial and name/place signs, which plain Unicode letters cannot reproduce.

sections.title: Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time

items.text: Cotton mantles, featherwork, greenstone, gold ornaments and warrior costumes arrived as tribute or trade and signaled rank. Maguey fiber served more ordinary cloth and cordage. Surviving luxury objects exaggerate elite life because damp soil destroyed most textiles; a gold ornament cannot stand in for everyone’s daily wardrobe.

Men commonly wore a loincloth and mantle; women wore a skirt and blouse-like huipil, with fabric quality, decoration and permitted styles shaped by rank. Dress also varied by region and occasion. Later illustrated manuscripts preserve valuable details, but conquerors’ labels and idealized figures require comparison with fragments, tools and sculpture.

Most commoner houses used adobe, reeds, timber and plaster around work or courtyard space; nobles occupied larger compounds. Neighborhoods included temples, schools, workshops and canal landings. Organic building materials and the colonial city erased much evidence, so the preserved sacred precinct should not become the floor plan of every home.

Farmers, fishers, canoe operators, porters, builders, potters, weavers, featherworkers, stonecutters, merchants, healers, priests and scribes kept the metropolis working. Palace storehouses also employed stewards and tribute officials. Many people combined seasonal tasks; a title in a manuscript may name an office without describing the holder’s entire day.

A carved teponaztli slit drum could sound at weddings, royal processions, agricultural dances or ballgames, and one example continued in use after conquest. Patolli and the ballgame mixed play, ritual and wagering. Nobody recorded every rule for us, so declaring a fifteenth-century “final score” would be magnificent nonsense.

sections.title: Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence

items.text: Nahua healers used plant preparations, massage, setting, steam, diet, prayer and divination in combinations that do not fit a simple modern split between medicine and religion. The 1552 Badianus Manuscript illustrates 185 medicinal plants, but it was composed and translated after conquest in a colonial college and cannot prove every 1490 treatment.

The Florentine Codex records named plants, drinks, washes and other remedies for particular complaints. Those recipes preserve Nahua knowledge and colonial-era practice; they are not medical advice, clinical trials or evidence that every treatment worked. Some ingredients may be pharmacologically active, while other explanations belong to a different theory of bodies and illness.

Midwives advised pregnant people, delivered babies, spoke ritual counsel and recommended steam-bath care in later Nahua accounts. The temazcal could support washing, warmth, recovery and ceremony. Book 6 was compiled after conquest, so its richly detailed speeches may be edited literary forms as well as evidence for practice.

Fresh water came from springs and aqueducts, yet access was unequal and many households relied on carriers. Bathing and steam baths were valued, but clean bodies did not make lake water germ-free. Canals mixed transport, agriculture and wastewater, and the city had no modern pressurized household network or universal treatment plant.

A scholarly sanitation study reports privies in public places and many houses, with excrement collected by canoe, while finding no citywide drainage system; organic wastes could be reused on chinampas. Much detail comes from early colonial descriptions rather than preserved toilet seats. Waste recycling reduced some pollution but carried health risks, history need not smell like a superhero story.

sections.title: The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not

items.text: The invasion beginning in 1519 was not a duel between Cortés and Motecuhzoma. Tlaxcalan, Texcocan, Huexotzincan and many other Indigenous forces supplied the great majority of coalition fighters and pursued their own goals. Internal rivalries, tributary resentment and succession politics made the alliance network fracture under pressure.

Smallpox killed Cuitlahuac and many others; blockade severed food and water; brigantines challenged Mexica canoes; fighting devastated Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco. Cuauhtemoc’s capture in August 1521 ended organized imperial defense. Disease mattered enormously, but it was one force within diplomacy, civil conflict, siege and mass Indigenous warfare.

Most detailed descriptions were written after conquest. The Florentine Codex joins Nahua testimony and art to a Franciscan program; the Codex Mendoza answers a Spanish viceroy’s questions; Spanish soldiers defended their deeds. Reading accounts against archaeology and one another reveals knowledge and bias instead of choosing one “perfect eyewitness.”

In 1531, Huexotzinco communities used eight painted amatl panels as testimony in a lawsuit over excessive colonial taxation. The document proves Indigenous scribes and plaintiffs adapted older pictorial accounting to a new court. It also warns against calling every Nahua opponent of Tenochtitlan a permanent friend of Spanish rule.

Imperial institutions were broken, temples destroyed and communities devastated, yet Nahua history continued through towns, families, land claims, manuscripts, worship, art and language. Mexico’s INPI today recognizes diverse Nahua peoples across many states and many language varieties. Living Nahuas are contemporary communities, not museum leftovers from an “extinct Aztec race.”

ending.text: The target feature ends at the 1500 atlas seam, but the historical Triple Alliance did not. The same polity immediately appears under the separate aztec-empire id and continued until the 1519 to 1521 invasion, Indigenous coalition, epidemic and siege broke its imperial government. Colonial rule then reordered land, labor, religion and political authority with terrible demographic consequences. Even that conquest was not cultural extinction: Nahua towns, language varieties, manuscripts, families, arts and political action continued. Because the 1500 endpoint is a database identity swap rather than a fall, this card records fell: null and creates no false successor state.
